title: Man Utd vs. Tottenham: High-Pressure Fixture Could Shape the Season
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By James Cormack2:00 AM EDTMichael Carrick suddenly finds himself under pressure. / Tiego Grenho/MI News/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesWe’ve not entered ’El Sackico’ territory yet, but there’s no overlooking the significance of Saturday’s Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur for both managers.
It’s a battle of the crisis clubs, as Michael Carrick’s 12th-placed Red Devils welcome Roberto De Zerbi’s bottom-of-the-table Lilywhites.
These two have struggled to escape mediocrity and outright incompetence for much of their recent histories, even if Man Utd haven’t yet sunk to the depths Spurs flirted with last term.

But there’s a sense that the Red Devils, after the highs overseen by Carrick during the second half of last season, are merely in the midst of an all-too-familiar cycle that will ultimately end with another manager losing their job.
As for Spurs ... well, they just want something to cling on to.

Carrick’s first full season was always going to bring about stiffer challenges. / CARLOS JASSO/AFP/Getty ImagesCarrick was robust in his response to talk of his potential firing before the break, labeling it “nonsense.” But that came before Man Utd’s draw at Craven Cottage, an indifferent display barely salvaged by Matheus Cunha’s late deflected strike.

It was a performance that drew fierce, hyperbolic criticism from prominent Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville, who said Man Utd’s early second-half performance against Fulham was the “worst 15 minutes” he’d seen from any Red Devils outfit.

Neville’s slander was predicated on the lack of effort and intensity shown by Carrick’s players, decrying their dynamism while they sat in a zonal 4-4-2 mid-block. But Man Utd’s walking out of possession is instructed. Carrick’s zagging, with an absence of man-to-man, while the rest of the division zigs with high-octane affairs predicated on out-dueling and outrunning the opposition.

And as Michael Cox pointed out in an article for The Athletic, league leaders Man City sit alongside the Red Devils with the joint-fewest high-speed runs and sprints. Liverpool and City have also covered less ground than United through five games. More running doesn’t equate to an improved performance.

Still, the role Neville and Co. play in shaping public opinion shouldn’t go unnoticed. They’re remarkably influential. Although plenty suggested Neville’s criticism was over the top, such comments can sow seeds of discontent, perhaps indirectly.

The modern-day manager has such a short shelf life, with results demanded from the outset. Clubs are desperate for their Jürgen Klopp or Mikel Arteta equivalent, but are so often unwilling to let the project marinate. We’re all so impatient.

And the job Carrick has taken on condemns him to win. "This is Manchester United Football Club we’re talking about here." His excellent work as interim manager was predicated on a common-sense approach that allowed United’s best player, Bruno Fernandes, to flourish. He didn’t reinvent the wheel, and nobody should ask him to either. It worked! No Premier League team earned more points last season after Carrick’s arrival than the Red Devils.

Bruno Fernandes thrived under Carrick during the second half of last season. / Catherine Ivill/Getty ImagesUltimately, he’s a victim of heightened expectations that are perhaps unjust, no matter the size of the institution he currently leads. His first full season at the helm was always going to bring about stiffer challenges with extra games, having benefited from free midweeks during the second half of last season.

INEOS rebuilt his midfield astutely, but was enough done in the summer to compete fiercely on multiple fronts? There are holes in defense, and Carrick is struggling to find the right attacking balance in the absence of Benjamin Šeško.

New issues are seemingly cropping up with each passing week, but Carrick has earned the right to be given the chance to fix them. Defeat here, though, and there’s no doubt that Eddie Howe, masquerading as the Grim Reaper, will feel as if it’s time to start knocking on the Manchester United manager’s door.

Club-record signing Sandro Tonali hasn’t yet found his feet. / Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesAnge Postecoglou may have provided one of the best moments in Spurs’ modern history, but at what cost? By sacrificing Premier League results in favor of Europa League prioritization, he paradoxically desensitized a club to losing. It became habitual.

The decision to part ways in the aftermath of Bilbao, ushering in Thomas Frank, proved horribly erroneous, yet plenty at the time understood why such a course of action was taken. Postecoglou was unlikely to ever build something long-term, even if he was one of the very few managers who seemingly understood what it meant to lead Tottenham Hotspur.

The extent of their demise last season meant an under-pressure and unpopular hierarchy felt they had no choice but to hand Roberto De Zerbi the keys. It took a mammoth salary and a guarantee of borderline total control for the Italian to take the job on, but it did pay off. Spurs remain a Premier League club as a result.
Yet by dancing with the combustible De Zerbi, questions have resurfaced regarding Spurs’ long-term outlook.
